name: DRV8220DSGR
title: DRV8220: 4.5 V to 18 V, 1.76 A single H-bridge driver; PWM, phase/enable or independent half-bridge control; autosleep; WSON-8 and SOT563-6
summary: A single N-channel H-bridge for one brushed DC motor, two one-way motors, latching relays, solenoids or other resistive and inductive loads, running from 4.5 V to 18 V. High and low side are about 500 mΩ each, peak current is 1.76 A per output (3.52 A with the halves paralleled), and the charge pump needs no external capacitors. The six-pin SOT563 version has a two-input PWM interface; the 8-pin WSON version adds a MODE pin for PH/EN and independent half-bridge control and an nSLEEP pin. Both sleep on their own when the inputs go idle, drawing under 1 µA, and both have undervoltage, overcurrent and thermal protection.

circuits.title: PWM interface motor-driving application for DRL package
circuits.description: The six-pin part runs one brushed DC motor in both directions. Two PWM outputs of a controller go straight to IN1 and IN2; the motor sits across OUT1 and OUT2. A single 0.1 µF ceramic from VM to ground is the only other part.
notes: Misprint: the VM, OUT1 and OUT2 pin numbers read 16, 15 and 14; they should read 5, 6 and 4.

circuits.title: PWM interface motor-driving application for DSG package
circuits.description: The WSON part drives one brushed DC motor both ways from two PWM lines. MODE is tied to ground for the PWM interface and nSLEEP to the logic rail, so sleep comes only from autosleep when both inputs sit low. VM has a 0.1 µF ceramic and a bulk capacitor; the thermal pad goes to ground.

parts.note: sized for the load and supply

circuits.title: PWM interface single-coil latching relay application
circuits.description: The same PWM hookup as the motor circuit, with a single-coil latching relay's coil across OUT1 and OUT2 in place of the motor. The relay is driven between forward and reverse, and between brake and coast. MODE is grounded, nSLEEP is on the logic rail, and VM carries 0.1 µF plus bulk capacitance.

parts.note: sized for the load and supply

circuits.title: PH/EN interface motor-driving application
circuits.description: MODE and nSLEEP both go to the logic rail, which selects phase/enable control. A plain GPIO on PH sets the direction and one PWM output on EN sets the speed, so only one PWM channel of the controller is used. Holding EN low past the autosleep time puts the part to sleep.

parts.note: sized for the load and supply

circuits.title: Half-bridge mode used as a high-side and low-side driver for two loads
circuits.description: With MODE left open the two halves work on their own. A valve hangs from VM to OUT1 and is switched by OUT1's low-side FET; a pump hangs from OUT2 to ground and is switched by OUT2's high-side FET. Each input takes its own PWM line, and the controller drives nSLEEP because this mode has no autosleep. In the worked example VM is 12 V, the valve takes 100 mA pulses of 100 ms and the pump 600 mA RMS.

parts.note: sized for the load and supply

circuits.title: Half-bridge mode used as a high-side driver with outputs paralleled
circuits.description: Half-bridge mode with both inputs tied to one PWM line and both outputs tied together, so the two high-side FETs share the current of one motor that returns to ground. MODE is open and nSLEEP comes from the controller.

parts.note: sized for the load and supply

circuits.title: Half-bridge mode used as a low-side driver with outputs paralleled
circuits.description: The paralleled half-bridge again, this time with the motor hung from VM, so the two low-side FETs together sink its current. Inputs are joined on one PWM line, outputs are joined at the motor, MODE is open and the controller drives nSLEEP.

parts.note: sized for the load and supply

circuits.title: Dual-coil relay driving, DSG package
circuits.description: A dual-coil latching relay has its centre tap on VM and one coil end on each output. Pulling OUT1 low energises one coil, pulling OUT2 low the other; the high-side body diodes catch each coil's flyback. MODE is grounded for the PWM interface and nSLEEP comes from the controller. In the worked example VM is 12 V and the coils take 500 mA pulses of 100 ms.

parts.note: sized for the load and supply

circuits.title: Dual-coil relay driving, DRL package
circuits.description: The six-pin part with a dual-coil latching relay: the centre tap on VM, the coil ends on OUT1 and OUT2, and a separate PWM line from the controller on each input. One 0.1 µF ceramic bypasses VM.
notes: Misprint: the VM, OUT1 and OUT2 pin numbers read 16, 15 and 14; they should read 5, 6 and 4.

circuits.title: Shunt resistor on GND pin of DRV8220 in the DRL package
circuits.description: The GND pin returns to board ground through a shunt, so the pin rises with motor current and that voltage is a current reading. A 1 kΩ / 100 nF low-pass takes it to an ADC input. In the worked example 150 mV across the shunt at a 1 A stall current gives 0.15 Ω, which keeps the GND pin well under the 0.5 V that the inputs' -0.5 V rating allows.
notes: Misprint: the VM, OUT1 and OUT2 pin numbers read 16, 15 and 14; they should read 5, 6 and 4.

circuits.title: Current sense amplifier example
circuits.description: For more range from a small shunt voltage, a TLV905I op amp in a non-inverting stage (gain set by R1 and R2) lifts the voltage at the GND pin before the ADC. The shunt and a filter capacitor sit from the GND pin to board ground; the thermal pad goes to board ground. The rest is the DSG PWM motor circuit: MODE grounded, nSLEEP on the logic rail, 0.1 µF and bulk capacitance on VM.

operation.text: Four N-channel FETs form one H-bridge, gated by drivers fed from an on-chip charge pump whose capacitors are all internal, so 100% duty cycle needs no external parts. The SOT563 (DRL) part has only the IN1/IN2 PWM interface. The WSON (DSG) part adds MODE, which picks PWM, PH/EN or half-bridge control, and nSLEEP.

MODE is a three-state input: low gives PWM, high gives PH/EN and open gives half-bridge control. Its thresholds are fractions of the nSLEEP voltage (internal 75 kΩ up to a buffered copy of nSLEEP and 130 kΩ down). MODE is not latched and can change while running. Its resistors draw no current from nSLEEP in autosleep.

The inputs accept DC or PWM from 0% to 100% duty. Each logic input has a 100 kΩ pulldown, so with nothing driving them the bridge is Hi-Z, except in half-bridge mode, where a floating INx gives a low output. Dead time between the high- and low-side FET of each half is generated inside.

IN1 high with IN2 low drives OUT1 high and OUT2 low (forward); the reverse pair drives the other way; both high brake through the low-side FETs; both low leave the bridge Hi-Z (coast). Staying in coast for tSLEEP sends the part into autosleep. This is the only interface on the DRL part.

Selected with MODE high at power-up. PH sets direction and EN switches the drive, so one PWM output on EN plus a GPIO on PH run a motor both ways. With EN low the bridge brakes on its low-side FETs; if EN stays low longer than tSLEEP the part goes to sleep and the outputs turn off.

Selected with MODE open. IN1 sets OUT1 and IN2 sets OUT2 directly, high or low, so each half can act as its own high-side or low-side switch for a separate load, give high-side braking, or be paralleled with the other half for one load. One half has half the on-resistance of the full bridge path and the two in parallel a quarter. This mode has no autosleep; sleep is through nSLEEP only. While one FET is off the other FET and the body diodes carry the freewheeling current, so no external diodes are needed.

In sleep the part draws IVMQ from VM. The DRL part sleeps only by autosleep. The DSG part sleeps by autosleep (PWM or PH/EN interface) or at once when nSLEEP goes low. To wake from autosleep, keep the INx pins (PWM) or EN (PH/EN) high for at least tWAKE, and only then start PWM. Waking with nSLEEP needs nSLEEP high for longer than tWAKE and the inputs out of their autosleep state. When autosleep is used on the DSG part, nSLEEP is tied to the logic supply. An nSLEEP left floating while VM is above VUVLO can produce unwanted outputs; a 100 kΩ pulldown on nSLEEP prevents it. Setting all inputs low before sleeping minimises system current.
First nSLEEP goes high; then IN1 or IN2 is held high for at least tWAKE, after which it may go low again or start switching.
Below VUVLO all bridge FETs turn off and the charge pump and logic stop. Operation resumes once VM rises back above the rising threshold.

Each FET has an analog current limit that holds the peak current down even into a hard short. A current above IOCP for longer than tOCP turns all bridge FETs off; after tRETRY they come back as the inputs command, and the cycle repeats while the fault stays. In half-bridge mode only the faulted half turns off and the other keeps running. The halves share one retry timer: a second fault on the other half before tRETRY ends holds both off for a full tRETRY.
Above TTSD all bridge FETs turn off. They turn back on once the die has cooled by the hysteresis, below TTSD - THYS.
VM follows the load's rating. For a brushed DC motor a higher VM gives more speed at the same duty cycle, and in any inductive load a faster rise of current.

operation.topic: Leakage with the load to VM
operation.text: In half-bridge or dual-coil use a load from OUTx to ground gives the least current into a disabled output. A load from OUTx to VM works but lets a small leakage flow into the off output (the IOUT rows). A load across OUT1 and OUT2 in a full bridge has no such leakage.

With the centre tap on VM, driving one output low energises its coil while the other output goes to VM, so the second coil carries no current. The high-side body diodes act as the freewheeling diodes. IN1 and IN2 both high would drive both coils, which a dual-coil latching relay must not see.

operation.topic: Current sensing on the GND pin
operation.text: A shunt between the GND pin and board ground turns load current into a voltage, which can be filtered into an ADC to detect conditions such as stall, or amplified first for more range. The inputs' -0.5 V rating, referred to the GND pin while board-ground logic sits low, caps the GND pin at 0.5 V. With the GND pin lifted, the logic levels must still meet VIL and VIH, MODE must meet VTIL, VTIZ and VTIH, and VM must stay above VUVLO. On the DSG part the thermal pad can join either board ground or the GND pin net. The RC filter is 1 kΩ and 100 nF.

How much local bulk capacitance is needed depends on the load's peak current, the supply's own capacitance and current capability, the wiring inductance between supply and driver, the allowed ripple, and the braking method. Too little lets the supply voltage move when the motor draws or returns current; more is better at the cost of size and price. The final value comes from testing in the system.

Use a low-ESR X5R or X7R ceramic from VM to GND, right beside the part so the loop stays small; the bulk capacitor, ceramic or electrolytic, also goes close. VM, OUT1, OUT2 and GND carry the load current and get wide copper. GND goes straight to the ground plane. The WSON thermal pad connects to the top ground plane, and through thermal vias to inner ground where there is one, with as much copper on it as possible.

The RθJA, ΨJB and ZθJA graphs are simulations on FR4 boards with 1-oz or 2-oz outer copper. Two 0.3 mm vias at 1.2 mm spacing with 0.025 mm plating sit under the part. On two-layer boards the bottom is a ground plane whose area follows the top copper. On four-layer boards the inner layers are 1-oz, 74.2 mm × 74.2 mm, one ground tied to the part and one power plane with no thermal tie, and the bottom has a pad the size of the package (2 mm × 2 mm WSON, 1.2 mm × 1.6 mm SOT). The top copper area is the swept variable. More copper, more layers and thicker copper lower RθJA and ΨJB.

Short current pulses such as motor start-up, an output short until overcurrent protection acts, or brief solenoid drive see a lower junction-to-ambient impedance than steady state. For short pulses the die and package set ZθJA; for long pulses the board does, and the curves for different layer counts and copper areas spread apart until they reach the steady-state values.

Dissipation is the sum of supply current loss, switching loss and conduction loss; other losses are small beside them. On-resistance rises strongly with temperature, so conduction loss is estimated with derated values. The junction estimate uses RθJA, which depends heavily on the board. Measured temperatures in the real system are more reliable than the estimate, and the junction must stay below its absolute maximum.
